B: Hiya! Oh, can you hear me alright? I'm never sure with this laptop.
A: Yeah, I can hear you fine.
B: Oh good. I'm Nicola, I'm in Eltham, South East London. How are you getting on? Did you do that puzzle thing at the start?
A: Erm, yeah. I'm Leanne. I'm near Peterborough, Whittlesey. The puzzle was alright, I sort of gave up on the last one, to be fair.
B: Oh, thank God, so did I. I sat there going round in circles and then the timer went and I thought, well, that's that then. I'm useless with them, honestly.
A: Yeah, I didn't really know what it wanted.
B: No, me neither. Here, I've got to ask, is that a Staffie in the photo behind you?
A: Yeah, that's Bella. She's my mum and dad's really, but she's sort of mine as well. She's getting on a bit now.
B: Ah, bless her. We've got one, Murphy. He's under the table right now snoring his head off, you can probably hear him. How old's Bella?
A: Thirteen. She's got arthritis in her back legs, so she's on tablets. The vet bills are, erm, they're not cheap.
B: Oh, tell me about it. Murphy's eleven and every time we go in it's another hundred and something. I said to Steve, my husband, I said that dog costs more than the kids did.
A: Yeah. Do you walk him much?
B: Every morning round Eltham Park before work, sort of a slow plod now. He sniffs every single tree. What about you, have you got somewhere nice?
A: There's a path along the river. I do the same loop most evenings. It's been really muddy this week though, she comes back filthy.
B: Oh, the mud, yeah. So what do you do then, if you don't mind me asking? Only I saw all them files behind you and I thought she's very organised.
A: Erm, I do the office side of my dad's business. It's heating and plumbing, he's got three engineers. So I do the invoicing, the books, booking the jobs in. That calendar's all the jobs.
B: Oh, that's brilliant. So you're the one keeping it all together, really.
A: Sort of. I'm technically a director, but that's mostly for tax reasons. I just do the books, do you know what I mean? Mainly I'm chasing people who haven't paid.
B: No, that's not "just" anything. I tell you what, the chasing is the worst bit. I work in a school office, primary school, and I do the dinner money, and you would not believe the parents who owe forty quid and look at you like you've made it up.
A: Yeah, no, I get that. Some of ours are months behind. I don't mind ringing them, to be fair, I'll just say it.
B: Good for you. I'm a bit soft, I always end up going, oh, don't worry, whenever you can, and then the head's on at me. Sorry, I'm going on. Is it nice working with your dad?
A: Mostly. It's the engineers who wind me up. They'll change a job round and not tell me, and then a customer rings asking where they are.
B: Oh, that'd drive me mad. My Steve's an electrician, self-employed, and he's exactly the same. He'll go, oh, I popped round Mrs Whatsit's instead, and I'm like, you was meant to be in Bexley!
A: Yeah, that's exactly it. I'd tell them off.
B: You should! So is it just you and your mum and dad then, with Bella?
A: Erm, yeah, I live with them at the minute. I moved back a few years ago. It's fine, it works.
B: Oh, it's lovely to be near your mum though. Mine's... well, I'm round there a lot. Do you get much time to yourself?
A: Not loads. Evenings I just do the dog, then telly. Friday's chippy dinner, that's about as exciting as it gets.
B: Oh, Friday's the best night. We do a curry, the Indian on the high street. What d'you have from the chippy?
A: Cod and chips, every time. I don't change it.
